science.title: Low overlap between bacterial and viral communities in meltwater and sediments of ice rise cryoconites
science.description: Cryoconite microbial communities are regulated by viruses and a wide range of functional genes linked to cold adaptation, yet interactions between sediment- and water-associated communities remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the microbial, viral, and functional diversity of meltwater and sediments from cryoconites on the Ward Hunt Ice Rise of the Last Ice Area. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed to assess microbial and viral biodiversity, while antibiotic resistance genes, virus-host matching and antiviral defense systems served as proxies for microbial interactions. Cryoconite holes host strongly compartmentalized microbial assemblages with contrasting diversity patterns. Bacteria, including filamentous Cyanobacteria and Actinomycetes, were more diverse in sediment, whereas eukaryotes such as dinophytes, green algae and rotifers were more diverse in meltwater. Viruses followed host patterns, with bacteriophages (Caudoviricetes) dominating sediment and giant viruses (Nucleocytoviricota) more prevalent in meltwater. Sediment communities also exhibited greater diversity of antibiotic resistance genes. These results demonstrate that meltwater and sediment aggregates from cryoconites support distinct biological communities and provide an initial baseline for future spatial and temporal comparisons.

science.title: Enhanced atmospheric radon forecasting using deep learning and advanced signal denoising techniques
science.description: The precise forecasting of ambient atmospheric radon concentrations remains exceptionally complex due to high-frequency noise and the non-linear behavior of its values. Although traditional statistical models like Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) are widely used, they often fail to capture complex non-linear patterns in high-resolution environmental data. This study presents a two-phase empirical evaluation of standard Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks with Digital Signal Processing (DSP) preprocessing techniques (FFT, Discrete Wavelet Transform, and Butterworth filter). Using a one-year dataset of hourly outdoor radon concentration measurements from Qena city in Upper Egypt, the impact of time-series denoising on model performance was evaluated across extended multi-step horizons (up to 24 h) and compared against Random Forest using Direct and Recursive strategies. The results indicate that applying a Butterworth filter significantly improves short-term predictive accuracy, allowing the LSTM model to achieve a test R² of 0.9668, while performance degrades sharply in long-term recursive forecasting. This research offers a robust, data-driven framework for forecasting outdoor radon levels, which could be adapted for other noisy environmental time series.
